title: Reading his good deeds to the Constitution publishers and a paper job
summary: Newspaper publishers are impressed by his good deeds, he gets a paper-selling job, substitutes for the teacher and jokes about a late honorary degree.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Yeah, so again that's what happened. As I say, and I got back into the class. I was in the head of the class again. And these people from the Constitution -- that was the name -- the publishers from the Constitution newspaper were there. And I had to get up. My time came. I got up and read some of my good deeds. They were impressed. It was kind of that nice intelligence, you see, because I

would choose these kind of good deeds that needs to be done, you know, like if a bird would be trapped in a tree, in a nest or something, or falling out of the nest or something like that, you know, because all the deeds were credits, see, and I explained this.

They was impressed, and they would let the school know, and the next thing I knew, I had a little extra job after school, you know, selling newspapers, which was the Constitution. I -- now, there was something about this paper I could continue doing. Being in the head of the class, again, I could read the paper, read things in the newspaper of importance, and my aunt had taught me how to write down things, you see.

And if it ever happens again, I'd get up and when my turn came to stand up and speak to the class, I would speak some -- I would read from my compositioning. And they were always impressed. And a good thing in those days would like, was, now, sometimes like the teacher when she wants to go to the principal's office or something, she would choose one of the students from the head of the class to like come up and, you know, say that -- take the teacher's place until she get back, you know, watch over the grade, the class, you see. So that used to happen.
And I got choosed, you see, I got chosen again. So I would always have something, some kind of entertainment

to do, like how to write on the chalk -- with the chalk, you know, write with the chalk, write -- ask a question, write down, ask a question in writing, you see, write it on the chalkboard, and I would ask everybody in the class, you know, in the grade now, "What is the answer," or something, you know.

And generally when the teacher would come back, I'd have all the grade, all the children, all the students in there, they would be laughing, you know, ha-ha-ha, and a lot of happiness, you see. So I almost got to be a teacher's pet otherwise. But it didn't happen, because I was taught how not to be spoiled, because like I say, my mother was very strict, and I actually found out where she got her strictness from, you understand. It was from her own mother, see.

And -- but the teacher liked that, and she would always talk -- she would tell the principal and so forth; they would come in there in the grade and question her about her -- her students. Who did she expect was going to graduate that year or something, you see?
-- I have to laugh because I didn't get a cap and gown until about like 52 years later, you understand.
And instead of being the Davis T. Howard school, it was the George Washington University, I mean. They made me honorary
professor, you know, master of taps, you see.
